newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Retail sales grab the limelight.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Retail sales grab the limelight.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will likely remain rangebound early next week as analysts brace for the release of key price and consumption data and a slew of fresh Treasury supply, analysts said.

They said January retail sales data, due out next Thursday, gained importance after the long-awaited January payroll report released Friday showed labor markets remained tight but wage gains were still subdued.
"Payrolls showed tight labor markets, but wage gains were limited. What people want to know is whether those small gains are being spent or saved," said a trader at a major U.S. investment bank.
Recent anecdotal data measured by the Lynch, Jones & Ryan's Redbook index showed that retail sales rose 0.8 percent in the first four weeks of fiscal January versus December.

Also providing an insight on consumer performance, most of the nation's biggest retailers, including Wal-Mart and J.C. Penney, posted sales increases in January. The gains, however, were mostly spurred by price markdowns.
Analysts said the anecdotal data seen so far suggest that retail sales might have picked up a bit in January, but not enough to trigger inflationary fears.
In a Reuters poll, Wall Street economists expected overall retail sales to jump 0.7 percent in January against a 0.6 percent rise in the previous month. The ex-autos data is seen up 0.6 percent.
"The key will be the retail sales data," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities. "But I don't think anybody is anticipating any overly frightening inflation problem here."
Players will have the chance to check how wholesale prices performed in January next Friday, when the government will release its Producer Price Index report.
Market participants will also have to cope with a new avalanche of fresh supply as the Treasury fires off its quarterly refunding auctions.
The government will offer the market $17.75 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday, $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.

Analysts said it was still difficult to predict how strong demand for the new issues would be. But they added that the scenario improved after the payroll report suggested wage inflation remains in check, at least for now.

"We saw the market performing well on Friday ... recovering some of the ground it had lost," said a trader at a foreign investment bank. "That could be a good sign for the refunding as far as demand goes."
Market players will also be keeping a close eye on the outcome of a meeting of top financial officials from the G-7 countries on Saturday in Berlin.
Money market players said U.S. bonds were likely to benefit if the dollar remained strong in the near future.
"The more important thing will be what, if any, kind of communique comes out of the meeting," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
The 6-1/2-percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted up 23/32 at 97-11/32 to yield 6.71 percent in late trade on Friday.
The Federal Reserve refrained from money market operations on Friday. Fed funds are seen opening at 5.25 percent on Monday. (( -- 212-859-1676 ))
